newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Bullimore looks set to reap rewards of survival.
newsitem.headline: Bullimore looks set to reap rewards of survival.

text.p: The story of solo sailor Tony Bullimore's rescue by the Australian navy last week may resurface in a book, advertisements and even a film in deals that could be worth more than US$1 million, his agents say.
But for now, the Briton has had enough.
Bullimore was reported by local media on Wednesday to have told his agents to put future deals on hold for the moment after a scuffle involving TV crews outside a Perth hospital on Monday.
"He would really prefer to do a few things without the media now," a spokesman said.

Bullimore, the centre of media attention since he was plucked from icy Antarctic seas last Thursday, planned a quiet 58th birthday party on Wednesday or Thursday night well away from reporters, the spokesman said.
The round-the-world sailor has already signed an exclusive Australian television deal, said to be worth up to US$100,000, and his agents are considering other opportunities.
Australian celebrity manager Max Markson, who said he has been working on Bullimore's behalf since speaking with his family, was optimistic about the shipwrecked sailor's potential.
"I guess he could make A$2 million (US$1.6 million) in the next 12 to 18 months," Markson told Reuters.
That should more than cover the loss of his uninsured boat, said to be worth about US$800,000.
However, the yachtsman's willingness to talk had probably ended the chance of an exclusive newspaper deal.
"There was a figure of 100,000 sterling (US$167,000) on the table last week but that fell over because he's done so many interviews," Markson said.
Efforts now are focusing on a book detailing Bullimore's several days beneath the upturned hull of his yacht in Antarctic seas, Markson said.
"The idea would be to rush a book out in the next couple of months," he said. A speaking tour was also possible.
Bullimore's dramatic rescue last Thursday with Frenchman Thierry Dubois created enormous public interest.
The winner of the television battle to sign Bullimore was flagged on Monday when he arrived in Perth wearing a cap bearing the logo of the local Channel Seven network.
Rival station Channel Nine said it lost interest when asked for 100,000 sterling for exclusive rights to Bullimore's story.
"We were never going to pay 100,000 pounds for someone who has since proved so happy to talk to everybody and anybody," a Nine spokeswoman said.
Markson said Bullimore's agents were talking with advertising agencies in Britain and Australia about using the yachtsman to sell chocolate, bottled water and tea.
Bullimore said he survived on "sheer determination, a little water and a little chocolate", while his first request on the deck of an Australian navy frigate was for a cup of tea.
Bullimore's British agents, Masters International, had invited chocolate manufacturers to link their products with Bullimore for 20,000 sterling, the Marketing Magazine reported.
However, advertising experts said Bullimore's potential was limited by the likely short-term nature of his fame.
"In a month's time it will be 'who is this Bullimore bloke'?", said Rob Clarke, managing director of Sydney advertising agency Leo Burnett Conaghan and May.
Possible movie deals have also been mentioned.
Markson said the U.S. film studio 20th Century Fox had expressed interest in the story.
Bullimore, meanwhile, continues to receive daily treatment for exposure injuries to his hands and feet and will remain in Perth for at least four or five days.
(One pound sterling = US$1.67)
